Stated Claim / Post Context:
Hurricane Isaias Brings 96 MPH Gusts to Florida as Flooding Threat Grows

Hurricane Isaias brought strong winds and heavy rain to Florida Friday night, with gusts reaching 96 mph reported at Pensacola Bay.
The post Hurricane Isaias Brings 96 MPH Gusts to Florida as Flooding Threat Grows appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Hurricane Isaias brought strong winds and heavy rain to Florida Friday night, with gusts reaching 96 mph reported at Pensacola Bay.

Fox News shared footage featuring FOX Weather senior correspondent Robert Ray reporting from Destin as strong winds moved through the area.

“Hurricane-force winds are hammering Destin, Florida,” the outlet wrote. “FOX Weather Senior Correspondent Robert Ray is braving the blast as dangerous Category 3 Hurricane Isaias bears down on the Gulf Coast just hours before landfall.”

The report showed the storm’s effects reaching coastal communities before its center came ashore. Isaias had strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane earlier Friday, but the National Hurricane Center’s 8 p.m. Eastern advisory placed it at Category 2 strength, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph.

FOX Weather’s subsequent coverage described the hurricane as making landfall along the northern Gulf Coast. Its report did not provide a confirmed time and location for the center crossing the shoreline.

Destin and nearby Fort Walton Beach were under a flash flood emergency Friday night as heavy rain threatened life-threatening flooding, according to FOX Weather. The outlet reported a wind gust of 96 mph at Pensacola Bay and a gust of 72 mph in Orange Beach, Alabama.

Water levels were also rising around Panama City and Apalachicola. Forecasters warned that storm surge could produce up to nine feet of inundation along portions of the coast between the Alabama-Florida border and Grayton Beach.

More than 365,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without electricity Friday evening, the Associated Press (AP) reported, citing PowerOutage.com. Officials in Mobile reported fallen trees and power lines, while Florida’s Emerald Coast Utilities Authority issued a boil-water notice for its customers.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned earlier Friday that residents should prepare for electricity failures and dangerous weather even outside the hurricane’s direct path.

“We prepared for the worst,” DeSantis said.

Evacuation orders were issued in portions of Florida’s Okaloosa, Escambia, and Walton counties, as well as Dauphin Island in Alabama. DeSantis, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey, and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp declared states of emergency ahead of the storm.

Forecasters expected the hurricane’s effects to spread inland through the weekend. Rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches were projected across southern Alabama, northwestern Florida, Florida’s Big Bend, and southwest Georgia, with isolated amounts reaching 15 inches.

The tornado threat was expected to extend into Georgia and the Carolinas Saturday. Forecasters warned that the most destructive conditions would occur near the storm’s center and to its east. Air travel was disrupted across northwestern Florida.

All Friday arrivals and departures at Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport were canceled. Pensacola International Airport recorded 74 cancellations, while Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport had 47, according to FlightAware figures reported by AP.

[Source 2 — nypost.com] (URL: https://nypost.com/2026/10/10/us-news/hurricane-isaias-hit-florida-like-a-freight-train-as-storm-leaves-thousands-without-power-lt-gov-jay-collins-says/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Hurricane Isaias hit Florida ‘like a freight train’ as storm leaves over 430K without power, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins says

Hurricane Isaias struck Florida "like a freight train" as the storm made landfall over the state's Panhandle and left more than 430,000 without power Friday night into Saturday morning, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins said.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Hurricane Isaias struck Florida “like a freight train” as the storm made landfall over the state’s Panhandle and left more than 430,000 without power Friday night into Saturday morning, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins said.

“This thing hit like a freight train. It was fast. It came in like a Mike Tyson punch,” Collins told Fox News on Friday night. “It’s real, I’m sure there is going to be real damage.”

Collins shared an estimated 900,000 people had heeded the warnings to leave Isaias path before it made landfall near Destin, Fla. as a Category 2 storm.

“While some might have ridden it out, if you have please hunker down, stay safe, let’s not put our first responders at risk and they’ll get to you as soon as humanly possible, but let’s let them do their job and remain safe as well.”

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone as it worked its way inland and maximum sustained winds to 35 mph, the National Weather Service said in its final advisory post on the storm at 5 a.m.

“I don’t think we’re going to have a Michael-like event here, we’re its just going to sit and have pockets of rain, thank goodness,” Collins said, referring to the deadly Category 5 that whalloped the Florida Panhandle on Oct. 10, 2018.

Preliminary reports didn’t show any catastrophic damage to the Sunshine State but Collins warned the storm isn’t over.

“The real extent of the damage as this thing crested and it hit shore, I think you’ll start to see good feedback coming through,” he said “We’re not hearing anything dire at this moment, God willing thats how it stays.”

The Republican leader, who has been in office since August 2025, revealed only power outages and radio damage have been reported.

Roughly 436,000 Floridians were without power as of 5 a.m. Saturday, according to tracker PowerOutage.US.

“We pushed really hard to have people listen to the evacuation orders, its just not worth the risk to you and yours,” Collins said. “You got to listen, got to lead and you’re going to live. It’s that simple.”

Collins applauded his leadership along with Gov. Ron DeSantis during the state’s preparations for the storm.

“We’ve led from the front. We have prioritized response in making sure we are on top of this,” he said.

Collins said over 5,000 National Guard were on standby along with 400 state guard.

Over 6,000 utility vehicles and people were prepared to help with power outages across the Panhandle.

“You got to remind people, once the storm is passed the risk is not over,” he said. “Don’t go out there, don’t get in water puddles or exposed water. Look out for power lines and remain safe. Use extreme caution.”
